clue.text: Percussive -crooning is monotonous

parts.note: crooning softly without words is humming
a drum is the classic percussive instrument

explanation.surface: Someone finds a singer's drum-backed crooning dull.
explanation.walkthrough: The charade runs in answer order: the crooning comes first, then the percussion.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dull and unvarying is described as humdrum.

clue.text: Possibly the ace of goddesses

definitions.note: the answer is one of the goddesses, the clue reading 'of goddesses'

indicators.note: possibly shows the letters could be arranged differently

explanation.surface: Some goddess might be the very best of them all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' turns THE ACE into the name; 'ace of goddesses' reads as the best goddess but means one goddess among them.
explanation.definitionFit: Hecate is the Greek goddess of witchcraft, crossroads and the night.

clue.text: The German kind may indispose you or me, like the French

parts.note: me is what either of us calls ourselves
as means like
les is French for the (plural)

explanation.surface: Some German sort might make you or me feel unwell, as could French cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The German kind' is German measles; this definition describes the disease that may make you ill.
explanation.definitionFit: German measles (rubella) is one type of this infectious illness, which can make anyone ill.

clue.text: May be drunk or pocketed at the bar

definitions.meaning: an extra fee paid to a barrister for continuing a long case

explanation.surface: A drink might be gulped down or slipped into a pocket in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the bar' suggests a pub; it is the legal profession, where barristers are paid extra daily fees.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a reviving drink and a barrister's additional fee for a case running beyond the first day.

clue.text: Paul screened one receiving about one cent — from Lady Bountiful?

parts.note: Paul Muni was a Hollywood film actor

indicators.note: about means going around, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: a fence is a receiver of stolen goods
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: An actor hides a woman taking in a coin, perhaps a gift from a generous lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts IC inside FENCE. Lady Bountiful is a byword for a generous benefactor, from a character in Farquhar's play The Beaux' Stratagem.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Bountiful is the type of a lavish giver, and great generosity is what one expects from her.

clue.text: Bit rare .perhaps for a judge?

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of the two words might be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A judge wonders whether a steak cooked bit rare is acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' turns BIT RARE into a new arrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: An arbiter settles disputes, acting as a referee or adjudicator.

clue.text: Survivor (or otherwise) of a forest fire

definitions.text: Survivor (or otherwise) of a forest fire

parts.words: Survivor (or otherwise) of a forest fire
parts.note: either a tree that came through the blaze or the grey powder left when it burned

explanation.surface: Someone escaped, or failed to escape, a woodland blaze.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is both a tree, which may survive, and the residue of burning, which is what is left if it does not.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a common forest tree and also the residue left after something burns.

clue.text: Outcry of one who has been fleeced

definitions.text: Outcry of one who has been fleeced

parts.words: Outcry of one who has been fleeced
parts.note: a swindled person's complaint, or the noise of a sheep just shorn

explanation.surface: A cheated victim protests loudly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fleeced' means cheated, but a shorn sheep has literally been fleeced.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the cry of a sheep and, figuratively, a feeble whining complaint.

clue.text: End-products of railway planning

parts.note: the stations at the far ends of lines, which are literally the ends planners produce

explanation.surface: The results of designing a rail network are assessed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End-products' means results, but here the products are line ends.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the stations at the end of railway lines.

clue.text: He didn't want change for a sovereign

definitions.text: He didn't want change for a sovereign

parts.words: He didn't want change for a sovereign
parts.note: not refusing coins for a gold sovereign but opposing any change of monarch or regime

explanation.surface: A customer hands over a gold coin and declines the change.
explanation.walkthrough: A sovereign was a British gold coin worth a pound; here it is the king, whom this supporter wanted kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A supporter of the king, as in the English Civil War, resisted replacing the monarch.

clue.text: Banter won't get you very far with a bird!

parts.note: chaff is light-hearted teasing talk
an inch is a tiny distance, so it will not take you far

explanation.surface: Teasing chatter is no way to win over a girl, the clue jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bird' is old British slang for a girl, which colours the surface; here it is a finch.
explanation.definitionFit: The chaffinch is a common European finch.

clue.text: Almost beheaded at dawn

indicators.note: with its head cut off, the word loses its first letter

parts.note: almost means nearly

explanation.surface: Someone was very nearly executed at daybreak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beheaded' removes the N from the front of NEARLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Something happening at first light is happening early in the day.

clue.text: Material some might say needed to finish the job?

indicators.note: signals that the word is pronounced like another, in some accents at least

parts.note: a tool is what a worker needs to complete a task

explanation.surface: A dressmaker reckons some fabric is still required to complete the work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some might say' hedges because the two words sound alike only in some pronunciations.
explanation.definitionFit: Tulle is a fine netted fabric used for veils and ballet skirts.

clue.text: Regular nuisance, the offender may expect?

parts.note: fair in the sense of proper, done by the rules
a trial is a troublesome person or thing

explanation.surface: A persistent troublemaker wonders what punishment awaits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nuisance' looks like a description of the offender; it supplies the second word. The definition is a description: what any accused person may expect in court.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone accused of a crime is entitled to an impartial hearing in court.

clue.text: Graft in the surgery ?

parts.note: graft suggests hard work or corruption, but also an implant: introducing a vaccine is a kind of grafting done at the doctor's

explanation.surface: Someone suspects corruption or hard toil at the doctor's practice.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a surgery is a doctor's consulting rooms. The word originally meant grafting a bud into a plant before its medical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The word first meant grafting a bud into a plant, and now means giving a vaccine.

clue.text: Going straight up in the air

definitions.text: Going straight up in the air

parts.words: Going straight up in the air
parts.note: read as soaring vertically, but meaning travelling in a direct line through the air, like a bird taking the shortest route

explanation.surface: Something shoots vertically into the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'straight up' suggests vertical motion; the phrase means the straight-line distance between two places.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes the most direct route, measured in a straight line rather than by road.

clue.text: Do they scorn the present?

parts.note: people who reject the present age and look to the future, as the early twentieth-century art movement did

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether the recipients despise a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'present' suggests a gift; it is the present time, which the Italian art movement rejected for the machine age.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian modernist movement led by Marinetti rejected the past and present in favour of speed and machines.

clue.text: Getting away from everything in space-it's fantastic !

indicators.note: fantastic means wildly fanciful, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone enthuses that escaping the world in outer space is marvellous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fantastic' scrambles SPACE IT'S.
explanation.definitionFit: Escapist entertainment offers flight from everyday reality.

clue.text: Retirement of extra girl out in a reshuffle

parts.note: super as a noun is an extra in a film or play
Ann is a girl's name

indicators.note: a reshuffle rearranges, so the letters of the three words are mixed

explanation.surface: A girl in a cabinet reshuffle is pushed out into retirement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reshuffle' mixes OUT IN A into UATION.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a pension or the state of being retired because of age.

clue.text: Not necessarily cycling salesmen

parts.note: the word sounds like pedallers, but these hawkers need not ride bicycles

explanation.surface: Some door-to-door sellers do not always travel by bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the near-identity with 'pedallers'; these travelling sellers may go on foot.
explanation.definitionFit: These are travelling sellers who hawk small goods from place to place.

clue.text: The alternative to defeat is in the air

definitions.text: The alternative to defeat is in the air

parts.words: The alternative to defeat is in the air
parts.note: read de-feat as in the doorway; the opposite of indoor is open-air

explanation.surface: Victory rather than defeat seems to be in prospect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the air' suggests rumour; it means open-air. The rest plays on 'defeat' and 'out' meaning beaten.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in the open air is happening outside rather than in a building.

clue.text: Regard for value

definitions.meaning: to think highly of, to prize

explanation.surface: Someone shows respect for worth.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun it means respect or admiration; as a verb it means to prize highly.

clue.text: Attachment to rock led to her undoing

definitions.text: Attachment to rock led to her undoing

parts.words: Attachment to rock led to her undoing
parts.note: in Greek myth a princess was chained to a sea rock as an offering to a monster, then freed by Perseus

explanation.surface: A fondness for rock music ruined some woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rock' suggests music; the rock is a real one, and 'undoing' is both her ruin and her being unchained.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ethiopian princess of Greek myth was chained to a rock until Perseus rescued her.

clue.text: Work 'over-time in the theatre

indicators.note: in a down clue, the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: op is the abbreviation for opus, a musical work
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A theatre employee does extra hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' places OP above ERA in the down answer; 'over-time' poses as overtime.
explanation.definitionFit: Opera is a staged musical drama performed in theatres and opera houses.

clue.text: Any householder these can move to tears

indicators.note: the letters can be moved about to form the other word

explanation.surface: Household bills are so heavy they can bring anyone to tears.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says these can be rearranged into TEARS; the parse runs the anagram back from TEARS. Rates were a British local property tax paid by every householder.
explanation.definitionFit: Rates were the local tax charged on property, paid by each householder in Britain.

clue.text: In appearance I'm something of a gent!

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe

indicators.note: only part of the words is taken, the letters running inside them

explanation.surface: A man claims that in looks he is quite the gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'something of' takes AGE from inside A GENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's image is the outward look or impression they present.

clue.text: Material for the matchmaker

parts.note: not someone arranging marriages but someone making matches to strike, who needs sulphur

explanation.surface: A marriage broker looks for suitable candidates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'matchmaker' is the maker of matches for lighting, and sulphur goes into their heads.
explanation.definitionFit: Brimstone is the old name for sulphur, used in making matches.

clue.text: Run to elude the keeper

parts.note: an escape from a gaoler, or in cricket a run scored when the ball passes the wicketkeeper untouched by the bat

explanation.surface: A prisoner dashes to get away from the guard.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the wicketkeeper stands behind the batsman; a ball beating both and allowing runs gives extras of this kind.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket it is an extra run scored from a ball that passes the batsman and wicketkeeper without touching the bat.

clue.text: Having a will of one's own

definitions.text: Having a will of one's own

parts.words: Having a will of one's own
parts.note: read as being headstrong, but meaning having made a legal will before dying

explanation.surface: Someone is stubborn and independent-minded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a will of one's own' suggests stubbornness; the will is the legal document.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who dies leaving a valid will is described in law as testate.

clue.text: Our remedy for unskilful playing?

parts.note: the whole is a quack's own remedy, Latin for ours

explanation.surface: A music teacher offers a cure for bad playing.
explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from Latin for 'ours', a quack's own secret remedy, hence 'Our remedy'. Read as two words it also says 'no strumming'.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostrum is a pet cure-all, originally a quack medicine of the seller's own recipe.
